tirade

/TY-rayd/ - rhymes with parade · noun

Hear It

What It Means

Tirade means a long, angry speech full of harsh language.

One wrong turn set the GPS-hating cabbie off on a tirade that lasted from the bridge to my doorstep.

Example

The retired general's commencement address slid into a tirade against 'soft living,' and the graduates' families were checking their phones by minute six.

A tirade is measured in minutes, not sentences: one voice, harsh language, no pauses for reply. A flash of temper is an outburst; a tirade is an outburst that refuses to end — the anger has found its rhythm and means to keep it.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

diatribe: A diatribe is a bitter, sustained attack that can be spoken or written — a review, a pamphlet, a speech. A tirade is always a voice: long, angry talk pouring out uninterrupted. Every tirade is heard; a diatribe may be read in silence.

screed: A screed is a long, tedious complaint, usually written — the twelve-page letter to the editor nobody finishes. A tirade is delivered live and runs hot; a screed sits on the page and runs long. Boredom is the screed's signature, anger the tirade's.

harangue: A harangue is a lengthy, aggressive lecture aimed at its listeners — it wants to browbeat you into agreement. A tirade is purer anger: it vents rather than persuades, and needs no point beyond the fury itself. You escape a harangue unconvinced; you escape a tirade deafened.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

toast: a short speech of goodwill and praise

eulogy: a formal speech honoring someone, usually in mourning

Where it sits · how long the fury keeps going — complaint → outburst → tirade

complaint vs. tirade: A complaint can be one calm sentence at the returns counter — the mildest ancestor of a tirade.

outburst vs. tirade: An outburst flares and is over; it stops short of a tirade, which sustains the anger for minutes on end.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — tir

Root — tir: to draw, pull, shoot (French tirer)

Suffix — -ade

Suffix — -ade: an act or product (as in blockade, escapade)

Put it together

Put it together: Tir (to draw or shoot) + -ade (an act of) = one long drawn shot. French tirade named an unbroken 'pull' of speech delivered in a single breath on stage; English narrowed it to the angry kind — one long volley, no reloading.

Use the root in a new word: retire

Use the root in a new word: retire: At nine sharp Grandfather would retire — literally draw himself back — to his study and his crossword.

Tirade names the speech, not the speaker's act: long, angry, uninterrupted. A brief flare is an outburst; a formal denunciation by vote is a censure (see this unit's reference list); and railing (this unit) is the activity — a tirade is often what it produces.
